Wireless Networks: Key Innovations, Challenges,
and Future Pathways

Abstract—The rapid growth in mobile communication tech-
nologies has turned mobile edge computing (MEC) into a
paradigm-shifting technology that extends cloud-like capabili-
ties and storage resources to the edge of the network. This
allows computation-intensive and latency-sensitive applications
to be performed in close proximity to the end-users, thereby
overcoming the bottleneck issues of resource-constrained devices.
However, ensuring efficient operations in MEC-empowered
systems requires intelligent task execution and resource allo-
cation across MEC servers. To this end, MEC-empowered
non-terrestrial wireless networks (MeNT-WiN) systems represent
a promising domain where deep reinforcement learning (DRL)

can serve as a powerful tool to enhance the MEC abilities in edge
servers and network entities. This paper presents a thorough
overview of the applications of DRL in MeNT-WiNs. In partic-
ular, it underlines the main contribution of DRL in enhancing
the performance of MeNT-WiNs, including autonomous aerial
vehicles (AAV) and satellite communications networks. This
paper investigates how DRL can meet the unique requirements
of MeNT-WiNs by enhancing system efficiency, scalability, and
decision-making processes across MEC architectures. First, the
article reviews the fundamentals of DRL, it later discusses its
integration with MeNT-WiNs and demonstrates its relevance for
the optimization of satellite communications and management
of AAV swarms, as well as enhancing connectivity in remote
areas. The survey also identifies key challenges for DRL-driven
MeNT-WiN systems, such as computational complexity and real-
time adaptability, while being scalable. Finally, it discusses
future research possibilities, emphasizing the importance of new
solutions that integrate DRL with MEC in order to fully exploit
the potential of MeNT-WiNs.
Index Terms—Mobile edge computing (MEC), MEC-
empowered non-terrestrial wireless networks (MeNT-WiNs),
deep reinforcement learning (DRL), autonomous aerial vehicles
(AAVs).

I. INTRODUCTION
RTIFICIAL intelligence (AI) [1] has witnessed a signif-
icant evolution over the past two decades, transitioning
from traditional machine learning (ML) frameworks [2] to
more sophisticated and powerful models. Early AI systems
predominantly relied on conventional ML algorithms, which
were designed to discern patterns from data and perform
specific tasks without the need for explicit programming.
These classical ML models, such as linear regression and
decision trees, were highly dependent on handcrafted fea-
ture extraction and predefined rules to function effectively.
However, as the complexity of real-world tasks increased,
these models struggled to capture the intricate structures
and latent patterns present in raw data, highlighting their
limitations and motivating the shift from ML to its subfield,
deep learning (DL) [3]. In DL, the key concept is the use
of neural networks (NNs) with numerous layers permitting
an automated feature extraction with a hierarchical learning
process. This hierarchical learning ability has made DL highly
effective in solving complex problems in areas such as image
or speech recognition, natural language processing (NLP),
and even mastering Go and chess, all without prior domain
knowledge. Because it eliminated the need for handcrafted
feature generation at scale, it allowed the creation of much
more flexible AI systems on top of problems that could not
be solved before due to their complexity.

and even mastering Go and chess, all without prior domain

feature generation at scale, it allowed the creation of much
more flexible AI systems on top of problems that could not
be solved before due to their complexity.
Building on the advancements in deep learning, reinforce-
ment learning (RL) [4] introduced a novel approach that
enables intelligent agents to interact with their environments
and learn optimal strategies using the paradigm of trial and
error, which enables AI to behave in such a way
as to maximize cumulative rewards over time. Therefore,
it achieves great breakthroughs in areas like robotic control
and strategic gameplay. Further evolution to deep RL (DRL)
widened these opportunities by merging the capability pro-
vided by deep NNs with those related to making decisions
based on RL scenarios. Such integration of AI models fur-
ther allowed the solution and acting upon more complex
unstructured problems while learning ways of navigating
them; this, in turn, will significantly enhance developments in
major evolving applications including non-terrestrial networks
(NTNs), industrial Internet-of-Things (IIoT), smart cities,
NLP, autonomous vehicles (AVs), and healthcare. DRL gives
the ability to make complex decision-making autonomous for
AI even in highly dynamic or uncertain scenarios. Overall,
the evolution from traditional ML to DL and from RL to
DRL marks the unabated improvement and extension of the
problem-solving capabilities of AI. This continuing devel-
opment opens up new areas in complex decision-making
and improves the capability of AI systems to act more
autonomously in a variety of applications.
The evolution of DRL has brought a revolution in many
fields, especially in the case of mobile edge computing (MEC)-
empowered non-terrestrial wireless networks (MeNT-WiNs),
where its capabilities proved transformative. In MeNT-WiNs
that include but are not limited to autonomous aerial vehi-
cles (AAVs), satellite-based communication systems, and
high-altitude platforms (HAPs), the use of DRL becomes
relevant due to its inherently dynamic and large-scale nature.
One of the critical uses of DRL in NTNs could be the
optimization of autonomous satellite operations by enabling
real-time decision-making of satellites for tasks such as orbit
adjustment, collision avoidance, and energy-efficient trajectory
planning [5]. Consequently, DRL enhances resilience and
efficiency in satellite constellations by autonomously assisting
with the management of complex tasks, particularly in low
Earth orbit (LEO) deployments, which are integral to next-
generation 5G and emerging 6G communication systems.
In turn, within the NTN network, DRL provides crucial
performance regarding the adaptive route planning of flights
and aerial surveillance. Such drones often have to fly in highly
dynamic and uncertain environments, whether over disaster
zones or areas with very sparse infrastructure. DRL gives
these platforms real-time learning and adaptation; hence, it
optimizes routing and communication links to ensure reliable
low-latency data transmission to ground stations. In resource
management within MeNT-WiNs, DRL significantly improves
spectrum and energy resource allocation for large-scale, decen-
tralized satellite and drone networks. Given the complexity and
diverse communication needs of MeNT-WiNs, DRL’s ability
to learn from experience and adapt in real-time provides
an effective mechanism for optimizing RF spectrum usage,
mitigating interference, and ensuring fair resource allocation.
In addition to this, MeNT-WiN’s cybersecurity has now begun
applying DRL since highly sensitive communication channels
need to be kept safe. DRL-powered systems are used to
predict anomalies, attempt to block cyber-attacks, and assess
network vulnerabilities, enhancing the robustness of MeNT-
WiNs from threats in a time of increased digital perils. The
integration of DRL into MeNT-WiNs increases not only the
autonomy and performance of those networks but also opens
new perspectives regarding innovative opportunities for remote
sensing, environmental monitoring, and worldwide connectiv-
ity. With its autonomous resource management capability and
adaptation to complex and dynamic environments, DRL surely
makes MeNT-WiNs play a key role in shaping future global
communications and enabling the next wave of intelligent,
interconnected systems.
Traditional optimization methods face significant limitations
in dealing with the complexity, scale, and dynamic nature of
non-terrestrial environments. These methods often rely on static
optimization techniques and predefined rules that face challenges
while adapting to the highly variable conditions and diverse
requirements of MeNT-WiNs. For example, resource allocation
schemes based on traditional optimization algorithms are typi-
cally computationally expensive and may not effectively respond
to real-time fluctuations in network demand or environmental
changes. In addition, such approaches often result in suboptimal
spectrum utilization, increased interference, and inequitable
distribution of resources among network users, especially in
decentralized systems such as satellite constellations and AAV
networks. Moreover, conventional security mechanisms in non-
terrestrial environments are inadequate to address evolving
threats such as cyber-attacks and data breaches because they
rely on predefined threat models. Similarly, traditional routing
and communication strategies often fail to provide low-latency,
reliable connections in dynamic scenarios such as disaster
recovery or remote sensing missions, where conditions change
rapidly. These limitations necessitate the adoption of more
adaptive, intelligent, and scalable solutions, positioning DRL
as a transformative tool for overcoming these challenges in
MeNT-WiNs.
Generally, DRL serves as a transformative instrument
for optimization, adaptation, and intelligent decision-making
extending beyond these general application domains. It
dynamically helps in the allocation of resources to accom-
plish energy-efficient content delivery in cloud computing
(CC) for optimizing server workloads and lowering power
consumption [6]. Similarly, in data centers, DRL enables
the effective routing of traffic that can reduce latency while
enhancing general operational efficiency [7]. In wireless com-
munication networks, DRL ensures profound improvement
in the efficiency of the spectrum, adaptive modulation, and
dynamic resource allocation, hence dealing with the random
traffic loads and diverse user requirements with minimum
interference [8]. Such optimization is imperative and indis-
pensable for meeting the high-performance demands of 5G
and 6G systems, as resource starvation challenges persist

A. CC
CC has emerged as a transformative paradigm in modern
computing, providing on-demand access to vast computa-
tional resources and storage without the need for direct user
management. This paradigm has played a crucial role in
supporting the exponential growth of mobile Internet traffic
and the increasing complexity of mobile applications. The
advent of mobile CC (MCC) extended these capabilities to
mobile devices, enabling remote data processing and appli-
cation execution at centralized cloud data centers. However,
despite its advantages, MCC faces significant challenges
in meeting the demands of latency-sensitive applications.
The long propagation distances inherent in MCC often
lead to excessive latency, which is unsuitable for real-time
applications like online gaming, virtual reality, and ultra-
high-definition video streaming [11]. Additionally, the rising
number of IoT devices and bandwidth-intensive services in 5G
networks has further highlighted the limitations of centralized
cloud architectures. Consequently, while MCC remains an
important component of modern networks, it is insufficient to
meet the stringent requirements of next-generation systems. As
a result, there is a pressing need for architectural innovations
that combine the scalability of CC with the low-latency
requirements of emerging applications.
B. MEC
To address the challenges faced by the CC, the European
Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) proposed the
concept of MEC, also referred to as multi-access edge comput-
ing. The ETSI defines MEC as a service environment where
CC capabilities are integrated with information technology
services at the network edge, especially within close proximity
to mobile users and the radio access network (RAN). MEC
decentralizes the cloud resources and moves the computing
power and data storage closer to the edge of the network, hence
creating an ultralow latency and a more reliable system. While
MEC is integrated with the RAN, mobile traffic can bypass the
traditional core network by routing data through the nearest
cloud-enabled edge server. This localized cloud infrastructure
reduces bottlenecks, improves base station’s (BS’s) computing
performance, and reduces potential system failures [12], [13].
Through decentralized cloud services, MEC not only improves
latency performance, but also expands the range of services
available to consumers, enterprises, and industries, making it
easier to deploy mission-critical applications. This paradigm
shift opens up new value chains, unlocks diverse application
scenarios in different industries, and effectively changes the
future of 5G and 6G service delivery. Fig. 1 shows the basic
architecture of a MEC-enabled system and demonstrates the
integration of cloud services at the network edge.
C. CC Versus MEC
There exist notable differences between CC and MEC,
as shown in Table II. They differ fundamentally in their
architectures, operational paradigms, and application scopes.
CC relies on centralized data centers, often located far from
end-users, to provide scalable computing and storage resources
over the Internet. While this centralized approach supports
high-volume data processing and large-scale computing, it
introduces significant latency and backhaul traffic due to the
long distances between users and cloud servers. In contrast,
MEC decentralizes these resources by integrating compute
and storage capabilities directly at the network edge, closer
to end-users and access points. This proximity enables MEC
to deliver ultra-low latency [14], reduce network congestion,
and support real-time applications that CC cannot efficiently
handle, such as autonomous driving [15], augmented real-
ity [16], and industrial automation [17]. In addition, CC
typically requires robust, high-capacity core networks to han-
dle traffic, while MEC mitigates this dependency by offloading
tasks locally, resulting in more efficient network utilization.
While CC excels at providing global scalability and resource
availability, MEC is designed to complement it by addressing
the latency-sensitive and localized processing requirements of
next-generation networks, such as 5G and 6G. Together, these
paradigms create a synergistic architecture that balances scal-
ability, efficiency, and responsiveness for diverse applications.
D. Computation Offloading Models in MEC Systems
Computation offloading is a critical mechanism in MEC
systems that enables resource-constrained devices to meet the
stringent requirements of modern applications by leveraging
edge servers. Offloading allows mobile devices to transfer
computationally intensive tasks to MEC servers, alleviating
their limited processing and energy resources. Depending on
the characteristics of the applications and their computational
demands, offloading strategies can be broadly categorized into
two types: binary offloading and partial offloading. These
models differ in their task partitioning granularity, complexity,
and ability to handle dependencies between task components.
In the following sections, we explore these models in detail,
highlighting their key features, use cases, and underlying
frameworks.
1) Binary Offloading: Binary offloading is a computation
task model tailored for scenarios where tasks cannot be
partitioned and must be executed entirely at a single location.
Specifically, such tasks are executed either locally on the
mobile device or fully offloaded to a MEC server. The model
represents tasks using a three-field notation X (M ; τ ; N ),
which captures the input data size M (in bits), the completion
deadline τ (in seconds), and the computational workload N (in
central processing unit (CPU) cycles per bit). These parameters
characterize the computational and communication demands
of applications and facilitate a straightforward evaluation of
latency and energy consumption. The task is required to meet
a strict deadline, ensuring completion within τ . However,
this model can be extended to accommodate soft deadlines,
permitting a small fraction of tasks to be completed after τ .
In this scenario, the computational workload N is modeled
as a random variable. Binary offloading, although simple, is
widely used in the literature due to its ability to effectively
model highly integrated or atomic tasks while maintaining
mathematical tractability.
2) Partial Offloading: Partial offloading, in contrast to
binary offloading, is designed for applications composed of
multiple procedures or components, enabling a fine-grained
division of computational tasks. In this approach, a program
can be partitioned into two segments: one executed locally
on the mobile device and the other offloaded to the MEC
server. The simplest representation of partial offloading is the
data-partition model, where input data bits are assumed to
be independent and divisible into separate groups for parallel
execution across different entities in the MEC system.
However, real-world applications often exhibit dependencies
among procedures, significantly influencing the execution
and offloading process. For instance, the outputs of certain
components may serve as inputs for others, mandating a
particular order of execution. Additionally, some functions
may be restricted to local execution due to software or
hardware constraints, such as image display routines. To
address these complexities, a more sophisticated task model
called the task-call graph, is employed, which is represented as
a directed acyclic graph K(V;D), the vertices V denote distinct
procedures, while the edges D denote their dependencies. The
task-call graph supports three typical dependency models–
sequential, parallel, and general–and accommodates detailed
specifications for computational workloads, resource require-
ments, and input/output data for each procedure. This model
effectively captures the interdependencies among components
and provides a robust framework for optimizing execution in

E. MeNT-WiN Architecture
Generally, MeNT-WiNs represent the seamless integration
of MEC with NTN platforms, including satellites (e.g., LEO
and geosynchronous equatorial orbit (GEO)), HAPs, and
AAVs. This architecture facilitates distributed computing and
low-latency processing, bringing computational and storage
capabilities closer to end-users, even in remote or underserved
areas. The MeNT-WiN architecture comprises several key
components. Non-terrestrial platforms act as mobile edge
nodes, hosting MEC servers to perform local computation,
caching, and analytics. Ground stations and the core network
provide backhaul support and coordinate with terrestrial infras-
tructure, while user equipment (UE), such as IoT devices,
mobile sensors, and smartphones, interfaces with the network.
Critical features of this architecture include real-time resource
allocation for efficient spectrum and power utilization, task
offloading from resource-constrained UEs to MEC-enabled
platforms, and adaptive network reconfiguration to maintain
performance under dynamic conditions such as mobility,
interference, and varying link quality. MeNT-WiNs are poised
to play a key role in next-generation wireless networks, with
immense potential for applications such as disaster recov-
ery, environmental monitoring, remote sensing, and enabling
global connectivity. Fig. 2 presents an illustration of a MEC-
empowered NTN environment.
The rapid evolution of wireless networks toward 6G
systems demands transformative architectures capable of deliv-
ering ultra-reliable, low-latency, and ubiquitous connectivity.
Traditional terrestrial infrastructures often face significant
limitations in remote, rural, or disaster-prone areas due to cov-
erage gaps, backhaul constraints, and scalability issues. In this
context, MeNT-WiNs have emerged as a promising paradigm
to overcome these challenges by integrating MEC capabili-
ties with NTNs, such as satellites, HAPs, and AAVs. This
integration facilitates distributed intelligence, proximity-based
computation, and agile service provisioning. By enabling edge
processing at non-terrestrial platforms, MeNT-WiNs signifi-
cantly reduce communication latency, alleviate core network
congestion, and support real-time decision-making for delay-
sensitive and bandwidth-intensive applications. Furthermore,
MeNT-WiNs are envisioned as foundational enablers for a
wide array of emerging use cases, including global IoT
connectivity, disaster recovery, precision agriculture, remote
sensing, and environmental monitoring. These capabilities
make MeNT-WiNs a critical component in shaping the
future of sustainable, inclusive, and intelligent wireless
ecosystems.

F. Challenges Associated With MeNT-WiNs
While NTNs assisted by MEC (or MeNT-WiNs) are
promising technologies for the next generations of 6G commu-
nications, they also face certain challenges owing to specific
mobility and propagation scenarios [19], [20]. Evidently, one
of the greatest needs is the optimal spectrum-sharing strategy
that should prevent interference between terrestrial and non-
terrestrial users, especially in cases of overlapping frequency
bands. Moreover, with the integration of MeNT-WiNs into
terrestrial systems, efficient management of shared spectrum
is essential in order to maintain network performance and
avoid interference issues. Furthermore, the significant path
loss in MeNT-WiNs, especially for satellite and HAP com-
munications, makes higher power demand inevitable to ensure
reliable signal transmission. This also poses a serious concern
on EE [21] issues, particularly when satellites and AAVs have
power-constrained devices.
Similarly, other challenges imposed on MeNT-WiNs include
latency [22], resource constraints [23], and variability within
networks [24], [25]. High latency is inherent in NTNs, espe-
cially for satellite-based systems such as LEO satellites and
HAPs, as the distances are long. Dynamic network topologies
from mobile platforms like LEO satellites and HAPs further
complicate service reliability. In these platforms, there are
also severe resource limitations, with confined processing
power and energy to support computationally intensive MEC
applications. Moreover, security and privacy concerns are
heightened by the wide geographic reach of NTNs, increasing
their vulnerability to eavesdropping and cyberattacks [26].
Furthermore, seamless integration between terrestrial and non-
terrestrial systems is essential for service continuity. However,
it presents challenges due to differences in communication
protocols and infrastructure requirements. This is an important
challenge to address to realize the full potential of MeNT-
WiNs in applications such as global IoT, smart agriculture,
and disaster management.
G. Limitations of Traditional Optimization Methods in
MeNT-WiNs
In the following, we discuss the key challenges posed by
conventional optimization methods, particularly highlighting
their inadequacies in dealing with the dynamic and complex

F. Challenges Associated With MeNT-WiNs
While NTNs assisted by MEC (or MeNT-WiNs) are
promising technologies for the next generations of 6G commu-
nications, they also face certain challenges owing to specific
mobility and propagation scenarios [19], [20]. Evidently, one
of the greatest needs is the optimal spectrum-sharing strategy
that should prevent interference between terrestrial and non-
terrestrial users, especially in cases of overlapping frequency
bands. Moreover, with the integration of MeNT-WiNs into
terrestrial systems, efficient management of shared spectrum
is essential in order to maintain network performance and
avoid interference issues. Furthermore, the significant path
loss in MeNT-WiNs, especially for satellite and HAP com-
munications, makes higher power demand inevitable to ensure
reliable signal transmission. This also poses a serious concern
on EE [21] issues, particularly when satellites and AAVs have
power-constrained devices.
Similarly, other challenges imposed on MeNT-WiNs include
latency [22], resource constraints [23], and variability within
networks [24], [25]. High latency is inherent in NTNs, espe-
cially for satellite-based systems such as LEO satellites and
HAPs, as the distances are long. Dynamic network topologies
from mobile platforms like LEO satellites and HAPs further
complicate service reliability. In these platforms, there are
also severe resource limitations, with confined processing
power and energy to support computationally intensive MEC
applications. Moreover, security and privacy concerns are
heightened by the wide geographic reach of NTNs, increasing
their vulnerability to eavesdropping and cyberattacks [26].
Furthermore, seamless integration between terrestrial and non-
terrestrial systems is essential for service continuity. However,
it presents challenges due to differences in communication
protocols and infrastructure requirements. This is an important
challenge to address to realize the full potential of MeNT-
WiNs in applications such as global IoT, smart agriculture,
and disaster management.

the strategies and actions of others. For instance, MADRL
can optimize the coordination of satellite constellations for

horizon dependencies and high-dimensional decision spaces.

structured framework that decomposes intricate tasks into a
hierarchy of manageable subtasks. This hierarchical approach
enables the system to operate at multiple levels of abstraction,

low-level policies executing specific actions. By leveraging
this structure, hierarchical RL enhances learning efficiency
and scalability, making it a powerful tool for tackling com-
plex, multi-layered problems in dynamic environments. This
structured approach not only enhances the scalability of
decision-making processes in large-scale MeNT-WiNs but
also improves resource utilization and system adaptability in
highly variable environments [43], [44]. By enabling efficient
task decomposition and execution, hierarchical RL aligns
seamlessly with the operational demands of MeNT-WiNs,
making it a critical tool for optimizing the performance of
MeNT-WiNs.
I. Different Perspectives of DRL-Empowered MEC
The rapid growth of IoT devices connected over the Internet
has led to the generation of massive datasets, including various
media types such as audio, images, and video. Given that
this data is produced at the edge of the network, it is
advantageous to analyze it locally. Techniques like ML, DL,
RL, and DRL are essential for efficient data analysis, quick
feature extraction, and learning patterns. Moreover, proper
scheduling and offloading tasks to edge computing resources
are crucial for effective data processing, ensuring specific
data requirements like quality-of-experience (QoE), privacy,
and low latency are met. DRL techniques offer robust data
prediction capabilities, making them suitable for accurately
forecasting data requirements and determining which MEC
nodes are best suited for processing. Below, we explore various
use cases of DRL-enhanced MEC from multiple perspectives.
1) DRL-Empowered MEC From Service Providers
Perspective: Bringing DRL models to the edge of the
network offers several advantages for stakeholders and service
providers. Processing data at the edge, where consumers
or nodes generate it, reduces latency and minimizes the
costs of transmitting it to remote cloud servers for analysis.
This approach is beneficial across various domains such as
safety, security, and marketing, including applications like
fire monitoring and user segmentation. Moreover, service
providers can optimize their long-term profitability by offering
computational resources to end-users. For example, in [31],
the authors introduced a public blockchain application within
MEC, aimed at maximizing the long-term profit of service
providers. In this context, miners offload their proof-of-work
tasks to MEC-operated BSs, and RL-aided frameworks allow
service providers to dynamically adjust prices per unit hash
rate while considering miners’ highest affordable price during
the mining process. The framework also allows miners to
efficiently optimize their strategies.

on integrating DRL techniques within MEC systems

include network slicing [56], [57], network function vir-
tualization (NFV) [58], [59], software-defined networking
(SDN) [32], [33], content caching [60], [61], network pri-
vacy [62], [63], and mobility management [64], [65].

to optimize networking technologies. These technologies
include network slicing [56], [57], network function vir-
tualization (NFV) [58], [59], software-defined networking
(SDN) [32], [33], content caching [60], [61], network pri-
vacy [62], [63], and mobility management [64], [65].
Network slicing, which decouples the physical network
infrastructure into several logical networks [36], allows for
more efficient use of resources. For instance, [36] explored
a 5G network slicing method using NNs and deep belief
networks (DBNs). In this method, attributes such as device
type and bandwidth are normalized and optimized using hybrid
metaheuristic techniques. This approach improves accuracy in
predicting slices like enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB),
massive machine type communication (mMTC), etc. The
hybrid method demonstrates improved accuracy over tradi-
tional techniques in simulations.
In NFV, which is a virtualization technology to manage
networking functions in software, the hardware costs are
reduced, and efficient service orchestration is ensured [34].
NFV enables functions such as traffic analysis and secu-
rity threat detection [35], and these services run through
sequences of service function chains, or virtual network
functions [66]. Although NFV presents several advantages,
challenges arise, particularly in resource allocation within
MEC systems. Offloading and scheduling service function
chains efficiently are crucial, as virtual network function
execution requires specific sequences. Several works have
explored these challenges, including [67], which provided an
overview of resource allocation challenges, and [68], which
proposed a DRL-aided strategy for service function chain
scheduling.
In SDN, the data plane is decoupled from the control
plane, enabling dynamic and centralized network resource
management [69], [70]. This improves network scalability
and efficiency while simplifying management tasks. The
integration of NFV with SDN in MEC networks has been
explored in several studies, such as LightMANO [71], which
presents a lightweight platform for managing network services
across distributed NFV systems. Other research focuses on
the convergence of SDN, network slicing, MEC in 5G
networks [72], and the fusion of MEC and cloud RAN [73].
The LayBack architecture in [74], facilitates resource sharing
across networking technologies, while [67] surveys SDN
and NFV relationships. Several other studies [75], [76], [77]
discussed the benefits of NFV and SDN within MEC systems,
particularly for ultra-low latency applications [78].
3) DRL-Empowered MEC From End-User Perspective:
From an end-user perspective, integrating DRL into MEC
systems offers significant advancements in meeting user needs.
DRL at the edge maximizes QoE by predicting user require-
ments. For instance, Facebook developed an ML inference
strategy for smartphones to minimize latency and improve
QoE [37]. Similarly, LiveDeep uses DL to predict the user’s
viewport in live virtual reality streaming [38]. In the healthcare
domain, HealthFog uses DL on edge devices to analyze
heart disease, providing healthcare as a service through IoT
devices [39]. Storing raw data on edge devices instead of the
cloud enhances privacy while providing real-time data analysis
for intelligent decision-making.
DRL techniques also allow end-users to offload latency-
sensitive applications, such as online gaming, and mobile
augmented reality to nearby edge servers or devices. For
example, a DRL-aided approach for task offloading in
mobile augmented reality applications is discussed in [38].
Additionally, a DRL-enhanced joint migration and task-
offloading approach proposed in [38] combined long-term
short memory (LSTM) and DRL for edge server load
prediction, enhancing the accuracy and speed of DRL models
during offloading. Table III summarizes the different perspec-
tives of DRL-driven MEC.
J. Related Surveys
Several surveys have been conducted to explore the appli-
cations of DRL and other ML techniques across different
domains of MEC and wireless communication networks. For
instance, the authors in [45] focused on ML-aided proactive
caching, emphasizing its role in AAV-aided wireless networks
and small cells. Similarly, Luong et al. [46] provided an
extensive survey emphasizing the DRL applications in wireless
communications and networking, underscoring its potential to
optimize network performance and adaptability. In [47], the
authors presented a detailed survey linking DL with mobile
and wireless networks, offering a comprehensive classification
of techniques, platforms, and applications, identifying key
challenges, and suggesting future directions for deploying DL
in mobile environments. Another survey [48], focused specif-
ically on the applications of DL in edge caching, presenting a
taxonomy of DL categories and caching principles for general-
purpose networks. Furthermore, in [49], the authors reviewed
the computation offloading problems in edge computing,
categorizing various approaches, including Markov decision
processes (MDPs), game theory, non-convex optimization,
Lyapunov optimization, and ML strategies.
Furthermore, the survey in [50] investigated ML-based edge
caching, presenting an ML taxonomy and content delivery
strategies. Although the authors offered a holistic perspective
on the role of ML in cache-aided networks, they allocated
limited space to discussing RL-based solutions. Similarly,
in [51], the authors conducted an extensive survey on resource
scheduling in edge computing, covering techniques such as
heuristic methods, approximation algorithms, ML, and game
theory. This work was centered on computation offloading,
resource allocation, and provisioning, however, it only briefly
considered the potential of DRL for these tasks. The survey
in
[52] delved into DRL-aided caching in heterogeneous
networks, however, the study merely presented the complete
taxonomy of DRL algorithms and focused primarily on fixed
cellular and cooperative networks. Meanwhile, the applications
of artificial NNs (ANNs) for wireless network optimization,
including edge caching, were explored in [53]. However, the
tutorial provided a limited discussion of ANN-aided edge
caching and referenced only a small subset of relevant studies.
Moreover, the authors in [54] focused on resource allocation in
MEC, assisted by ML and DL, however, the authors narrowed
their scope to a subset of IoT networks, leaving gaps in the
broader exploration of ML and DL’s full potential in MEC.

dedicated to optimizing MEC and wireless communication
systems through ML, DL, and DRL, while also highlighting
areas where further exploration, particularly in task offloading

and wireless networks, offering a comprehensive classification
of techniques, platforms, and applications, identifying key
challenges, and suggesting future directions for deploying DL
in mobile environments. Another survey [48], focused specif-
ically on the applications of DL in edge caching, presenting a
taxonomy of DL categories and caching principles for general-
purpose networks. Furthermore, in [49], the authors reviewed
the computation offloading problems in edge computing,
categorizing various approaches, including Markov decision
processes (MDPs), game theory, non-convex optimization,
Lyapunov optimization, and ML strategies.
Furthermore, the survey in [50] investigated ML-based edge
caching, presenting an ML taxonomy and content delivery
strategies. Although the authors offered a holistic perspective
on the role of ML in cache-aided networks, they allocated
limited space to discussing RL-based solutions. Similarly,
in [51], the authors conducted an extensive survey on resource
scheduling in edge computing, covering techniques such as
heuristic methods, approximation algorithms, ML, and game
theory. This work was centered on computation offloading,
resource allocation, and provisioning, however, it only briefly
considered the potential of DRL for these tasks. The survey
in
[52] delved into DRL-aided caching in heterogeneous
networks, however, the study merely presented the complete
taxonomy of DRL algorithms and focused primarily on fixed
cellular and cooperative networks. Meanwhile, the applications
of artificial NNs (ANNs) for wireless network optimization,
including edge caching, were explored in [53]. However, the
tutorial provided a limited discussion of ANN-aided edge
caching and referenced only a small subset of relevant studies.
Moreover, the authors in [54] focused on resource allocation in
MEC, assisted by ML and DL, however, the authors narrowed
their scope to a subset of IoT networks, leaving gaps in the
broader exploration of ML and DL’s full potential in MEC.
Collectively, these surveys reflect the growing body of work
dedicated to optimizing MEC and wireless communication
systems through ML, DL, and DRL, while also highlighting
areas where further exploration, particularly in task offloading
and resource management, remains necessary. The surveys
conducted in [79], [80], [53], [81] are relevant to networking,
however, they are targeting the applications of ML and DL
in specific network areas. Furthermore, the survey conducted
in [82] discusses the application of DRL in NTN in 6G
communication networks. The survey in [55] presented the
applications of DRL in MEC-empowered terrestrial networks
specifically focusing on terrestrial IoT and vehicular networks.

Despite significant advancements in communication tech-
nologies, the aforementioned studies have primarily focused
on ML/DL-enhanced IoT or DRL-enhanced communication,
with limited exploration of their applications in NTNs.
Specifically, prior works rarely explore the potential of inte-
grating MEC with DRL-empowered NTNs and hardly provide
a comprehensive analysis of DRL-enhanced NTNs empowered
by MEC. Traditional optimization methods used in NTNs
face inherent limitations, including their inability to handle
the scalability, adaptability, and real-time decision-making
demands of these networks. As a result, these methods often
lead to suboptimal resource allocation, inefficient spectrum
utilization, and inadequate energy management–key challenges
that remain unresolved in the context of NTNs. DRL has
emerged as a powerful solution to address these limita-
tions by offering unique capabilities for optimizing resource
management, spectrum allocation, and security in complex
and dynamic environments. Recent advances in DRL have
demonstrated its ability to adapt to non-terrestrial settings,
optimize multi-objective problems, and make intelligent, real-
time decisions, thereby overcoming the challenges posed by
traditional approaches. Motivated by these developments, this
survey delves into the integration of DRL with MEC-enabled
NTNs, with particular emphasis on optimizing resource allo-
cation, enhancing EE, and improving system adaptability.
Unlike previous works that primarily focus on terrestrial-
centric applications [55], this survey highlights the unique
challenges and opportunities associated with DRL in MeNT-
WiNs, such as satellite communications and HAPs. It also
addresses a critical gap in the existing literature by exploring
innovative approaches to integrate DRL within MeNT-WiNs,
particularly how DRL can transform resource management,
spectrum efficiency, and energy consumption in non-terrestrial
environments. By focusing on these aspects, this survey
provides a broader and more comprehensive perspective on
DRL applications in MeNT-WiNs. A comparative analysis
of this survey with existing works is provided in Table IV,
highlighting its contribution to filling the research gap in DRL-
assisted MEC-enabled NTN networks and paving the way for
future innovations in next-generation wireless networks.
K. Key Contributions
In this article, we present a state-of-the-art survey focusing
specifically on the applications of DRL in MeNT-WiN. This
comprehensive survey offers a focused examination of DRL’s
transformative role in NTNs, filling a critical gap in the
existing literature and paving the way for future innovations in
this rapidly evolving field. Accordingly, our key contributions
are summarized as follows:
• We establish a structured framework that systematically
explores the applications of DRL within the context of
MEC-empowered NT-WiNs (or MeNT-WiNs), examining
its impact on optimizing resource management, com-
munication efficiency, and decision-making processes in
satellite communication and AAV-based networks.
• The survey provides an in-depth exploration of the foun-
dational principles of DRL, offering a clear understanding
of the essential concepts governing its application in
NTNs, particularly in enhancing the adaptability and effi-
ciency of these dynamic, and decentralized environments.
• We thoroughly examine the integration of DRL into
MeNT-WiNs, showcasing its effectiveness in optimizing
satellite systems, improving AAV network performance,
and enabling advanced decision-making in challenging,
high-mobility, and high-latency environments character-
istic of MeNT-WiNs.
We present and discuss the unique challenges faced
while applying DRL in MeNT-WiNs, including scal-
ability, computational complexity, robust performance,
and energy-efficient communication. Additionally, we
identify emerging trends and outline future research
directions, providing a roadmap for advancing the field
of DRL in MeNT-WiNs and guiding future developments
in 6G communications and beyond.

II. FUNDAMENTALS OF AI
This section introduces the foundational principles of AI,
guiding the reader through relevant concepts in AI, ML, DL,
and RL, and ultimately leading to various DRL techniques.
These techniques leverage the power of DL to enhance
network performance and efficiency. We begin by discussing
AI and its key subcategories, each adopting different learning
methodologies, resulting in distinct branches.
A. AI.
AI encompasses the creation of computer systems that
perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, like
problem-solving, decision-making, learning, and language pro-
cessing. AI strives to construct machines that can replicate
human cognitive functions, allowing them to analyze data,
adapt to dynamic environments, and make autonomous deci-
sions. Techniques such as ML, DL, RL, DRL, and NLP
are employed to enhance these systems, enabling them to
learn from experience. Applications of AI span numerous
sectors, including smart industries [83], AVs [84], [85],
smart transportation [86], [87], healthcare [88], [89], [90],
finance [91], [92], [93], agriculture [94], [95], [96], and smart
cities [97], [98], [99], [100]. Consequently, AI is revolutioniz-
ing diverse fields, driving innovation, and reshaping the world.

B. ML
As a subfield of AI, ML, aims to design algorithms that
enable systems to learn from data and improve performance
over time without being explicitly programmed. ML’s strength
lies in identifying patterns, making predictions, and extracting
insights from data, thus allowing systems to adapt dynamically
to new information [101], [2]. This iterative learning process
makes ML particularly effective across various domains, such
as healthcare, where it assists in diagnostics and personalized
treatment plans [102], and finance, where it plays a key role
in risk assessment and fraud detection [103]. Furthermore,
ML powers image and speech recognition [104], [105], and
recommendation systems, enhancing user experience across
digital platforms [106]. Below, we discuss two types of ML
models.
1) Supervised Learning: In supervised learning, a data set,
containing features (or inputs) and the corresponding outputs,
is supplied to the model for training, thereby called supervised
learning. The model is trained over several iterations to
learn how to map given inputs to outputs. The model uses
the given labeled outputs to improve its performance by
conducting a comparison between the actual and predicted
output [107]. Supervised learning is further classified as,
i) regression, and ii) classification. The regression analy-
sis examines the relationship between a dependent variable
and one or more independent variables using a statistical
method. This method minimizes the error between expected
and actual outputs to derive the functional mapping between
inputs and outputs. Furthermore, the output label in the
case of regression can assume continuous values [108]. On
the other hand, in classification, the given output labels
represent distinct classes defined in image classification,
Typically, classification problems are addressed by employ-
ing probabilistic classifiers to map output classes based on
inputs, for instance, the naive Bayes classifier [110]. The
supervised learning algorithms for the ML paradigm include
linear regression [111], logistic regression [112], support
vector machine (SVM) [113], Naive Bayes model [110],
and decision tree [114]. Similarly, the supervised learning
algorithms for the DL paradigm include perceptron [115],
multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or fully connected NNs
(FNNs) [116], extreme learning machine [117], deep residual
network (DRN) [118], connected NNs [119], deconvolu-
tional network [120], probabilistic NNs [121], recurrent
NNs [122], [123], LSTM [124], reservoir computing [125],
gated recurrent units, and transformers [126].
2) Unsupervised Learning: Unlike supervised learning,
where models are trained with labeled datasets to learn a
direct input-output mapping, unsupervised learning operates
on datasets that contain only input features, with no associated
output labels. While supervised learning aims to learn a direct
mapping from inputs to known outputs, unsupervised learning
seeks to discover hidden patterns, groupings, or underlying
structures within the data [127]. Since the data does not come
with predefined output labels, the learning objective is to
identify similarities, groupings, or latent representations that
describe the data distribution.

the input data to infer relationships or organization based
on statistical properties. A key example is clustering, where
the model identifies groups of similar data points based on

B. ML
As a subfield of AI, ML, aims to design algorithms that
enable systems to learn from data and improve performance
over time without being explicitly programmed. ML’s strength
lies in identifying patterns, making predictions, and extracting
insights from data, thus allowing systems to adapt dynamically
to new information [101], [2]. This iterative learning process
makes ML particularly effective across various domains, such
as healthcare, where it assists in diagnostics and personalized
treatment plans [102], and finance, where it plays a key role
in risk assessment and fraud detection [103]. Furthermore,
ML powers image and speech recognition [104], [105], and
recommendation systems, enhancing user experience across
digital platforms [106]. Below, we discuss two types of ML
models.
1) Supervised Learning: In supervised learning, a data set,
containing features (or inputs) and the corresponding outputs,
is supplied to the model for training, thereby called supervised
learning. The model is trained over several iterations to
learn how to map given inputs to outputs. The model uses
the given labeled outputs to improve its performance by
conducting a comparison between the actual and predicted
output [107]. Supervised learning is further classified as,
i) regression, and ii) classification. The regression analy-
sis examines the relationship between a dependent variable
and one or more independent variables using a statistical
method. This method minimizes the error between expected
and actual outputs to derive the functional mapping between
inputs and outputs. Furthermore, the output label in the
case of regression can assume continuous values [108]. On
the other hand, in classification, the given output labels
represent distinct classes defined in image classification,
Typically, classification problems are addressed by employ-
ing probabilistic classifiers to map output classes based on
inputs, for instance, the naive Bayes classifier [110]. The
supervised learning algorithms for the ML paradigm include
linear regression [111], logistic regression [112], support
vector machine (SVM) [113], Naive Bayes model [110],
and decision tree [114]. Similarly, the supervised learning
algorithms for the DL paradigm include perceptron [115],
multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or fully connected NNs
(FNNs) [116], extreme learning machine [117], deep residual
network (DRN) [118], connected NNs [119], deconvolu-
tional network [120], probabilistic NNs [121], recurrent
NNs [122], [123], LSTM [124], reservoir computing [125],
gated recurrent units, and transformers [126].
2) Unsupervised Learning: Unlike supervised learning,
where models are trained with labeled datasets to learn a
direct input-output mapping, unsupervised learning operates
on datasets that contain only input features, with no associated
output labels. While supervised learning aims to learn a direct
mapping from inputs to known outputs, unsupervised learning
seeks to discover hidden patterns, groupings, or underlying
structures within the data [127]. Since the data does not come
with predefined output labels, the learning objective is to
identify similarities, groupings, or latent representations that
describe the data distribution.
Since no labels are provided, the algorithm must analyze
the input data to infer relationships or organization based
on statistical properties. A key example is clustering, where
the model identifies groups of similar data points based on
feature similarity. Another important task is dimensionality
reduction, which projects high-dimensional data into lower-
dimensional representations while retaining key structural
information. These unsupervised techniques are often used
for data exploration, feature extraction, and as pre-processing
steps in broader ML workflows.

C. Federated Learning (FL)
In FL, the training of the model occurs across multiple
devices or servers holding local data without sharing the
raw data itself [142]. Clients (devices) collaborate under
the supervision of a central server, which aggregates locally
computed updates into a global model. FL ensures data
privacy and security by keeping data localized, making it
particularly effective in scenarios where privacy concerns are
paramount. In edge computing environments, FL models can
learn global patterns while leveraging data stored locally
on each device, enabling applications such as mobile edge
popularity prediction [143].
D. DL
DL, another branch of AI, builds upon ML by using NNs to
address complex tasks where feature extraction is challenging.
DL leverages NNs to model high-dimensional data [144], as
they consist of layers of interconnected nodes, called neurons,
which mimic the architecture of the human brain [145].
The multiple layers within these networks allow DL to
uncover intricate patterns and relationships in data. Neurons
are connected via edges assigned weights, which are iteratively
optimized through backpropagation algorithms [146]. The
learning process in DL often involves minimizing a cost
function (representing the difference between predicted and
actual outputs) using optimization techniques like stochastic
gradient descent (GD) [147], [148], Newton’s method [149],
and GD [150], allowing the system to learn complex repre-
sentations. Fig. 4 (a) presents an illustration of DL.
E. RL
RL is an experience-driven learning approach where an
agent learns by interacting with an environment rather than
relying on a predefined dataset. The agent receives rewards or
penalties based on the actions it takes within the environment,
allowing it to improve its behavior over time [151]. The envi-
ronment is often modeled using the MDP [152], which offers
a mathematical framework for decision-making in stochastic
scenarios. The aim of RL is to discover a policy that minimizes
penalties (or maximizes cumulative rewards) over a specified
time horizon, based on the agent’s state. Fig. 4 (b) illustrates
the basic components of an RL system.
F. DRL
DRL, first introduced in [153], merges the strengths of DL
and RL, making it well-suited for complex, high-dimensional
problems. While traditional RL algorithms are effective for
environments with limited state and action spaces, they
struggle when applied to real-world scenarios that involve
continuous or high-dimensional spaces. As finding an optimal
policy in such environments becomes increasingly challenging,
DRL was developed to overcome this limitation by effi-
ciently handling high-dimensional data and continuous action
spaces. In DRL, the RL framework consists of a self-learning
agent that maximizes long-term rewards without requiring a
model of the environment. At the same time, DL, inspired
by biological NNs, plays a critical role in addressing the
complexities inherent in these environments, enabling the
agent to extract meaningful features from large state spaces.

H. DRL Models Classification
Based on the wide variety of DRL applications, several DRL
algorithm variations have emerged, primarily distinguished by
whether they rely on a predefined model or not. As a result,
DRL methods are generally categorized into two main classes:
model-based DRL methods and model-free DRL methods.
Below we discuss these categories in detail. Fig. 6 depicts the
different classes of DRL algorithms.
1) Model-Based DRL Methods: In model-based DRL
methods, the agent constructs a model based on feedback
obtained from the environment. This model is then used
to predict the impact of actions on the states and rewards,
allowing the agent to derive an optimal policy. Examples of
model-based methods include AlphaZero [166], model-based
RL with model-free fine-tuning (MBMF) [167], imagination-
augmented agents (I2A) [168], and monte carlo tree search
(MCTS) [169]. Model-based strategies typically exhibit lower
sample complexity, as they reduce the need for extensive
interactions with the environment. However, if the model is
inaccurate, the resulting policy may be suboptimal, leading to
less precise and suboptimal outcomes.
2) Model-Free DRL Methods: In model-free DRL meth-
ods, the agents learn optimal policies by directly interacting
with the environment, without structuring a model of the
dynamics of the environment. These methods are further
categorized into different approaches based on how they learn
from the interaction.

• Actor-Critic Methods: In this class of DRL algorithms,
the attributes of both policy and value-based approaches
are combined. These methods employ two NNs: the
actor network and the critic network. The actor network
operates similarly to the NN in policy-based meth-
ods, while the critic network functions like those in
value-based methods. In the actor-critic architecture, the
actor network is responsible for selecting actions that
maximize the expected cumulative reward over time.
Whereas, the critic network evaluates the quality of
the actions taken by the actor by computing the value
function. A feedback loop is integral to these meth-
ods, where the critic provides feedback to the actor
by assessing the expected cumulative reward of being
in a particular state and following the actor’s policy
thereafter. In essence, the critic network optimizes the
parameters of the value functions based on the actor’s
policy. Simultaneously, the actor network updates its
policy parameters using the value function evaluations
provided by the critic. Examples of actor-critic algorithms

III. DRL IN MENT-WINS
MEC is envisioned as a promising solution to address the
high demand for high-throughput and low-latency applications
in wireless communication networks. In the context of non-
terrestrial environments such as AAVs, satellite networks, and
aerial drones, MEC offers the potential to bring storage and
computation capabilities closer to the edge of the network,
enabling faster response times and improved user experi-
ences. However, the effective utilization of MEC resources
in NT-WiNs faces challenges due to factors like intermittent
connectivity, limited bandwidth, and dynamic environmental
conditions. In the recent past, DRL has gained traction as a
powerful tool to address certain challenges faced by wireless
communication networks, for instance, resource allocation
optimization, enhancing EE, improving QoS, task offload-
ing, addressing security concerns, and network optimization.
Together with MEC, DRL can offer the opportunity to enhance
the performance of wireless communication networks, specif-
ically the NTNs.
This section provides a detailed review of existing litera-
ture on DRL-assisted MEC in NT-WiNs particularly, related
to resource allocation, EE, QoS improvement, task offload-
ing, and security and privacy. This section explains how
DRL-enabled MEC can bring transformative changes to com-
munication systems in non-terrestrial settings, unlocking new
opportunities for applications and services by synthesizing
insights from diverse studies.
A. Resource Allocation
In general, resource allocation is a key issue in MeNT-WiNs,
where computing, storage, and communication resources have
to be used efficiently to optimize network performance for
diversified applications and services. Recently, DRL has been
considered an attractive paradigm for dynamic resource allo-
cation in the network edge, as it has the capability to learn and
discover the optimal policies that eventually lead to optimal
decision-making while interacting with the environment. This
subsection highlights a review of the existing literature related
to DRL-assisted resource allocation strategies in MeNT-WiNs.
We look into how DRL algorithms are being implemented
for effective resource allocation adaptable to dynamic network
conditions, traffic patterns, and user demands with the view
to maximizing resource utilization, latency minimization, and
optimizing network efficiency. The following subsection syn-
thesizes insights from studies conducted within a wide range,
with the aim of presenting an extended review to understand
the state-of-the-art approaches in DRL-enhanced resource
allocation for MeNT-WiNs.
The authors in [193] formulated a joint optimization
problem that addressed both computation offloading and
resource allocation in a MEC-empowered integrated aerial-
terrestrial vehicular network. They modeled the problem as an
MDP, which captured the stochastic nature of the environment,
including the variability in user demands, communication
channel conditions, and computational workloads. Using their
concept of minimizing the total overhead of computation in
the network, they proposed a DDQL-based solution. In the
system, every vehicle corresponded to some intelligent agent
that interacted with an unknown and dynamic environment to
learn its best policy in an adaptive manner. The DDQL-based
solution harnessed DQL to optimize primary parameters, such
as offloading computation decisions and resource allocation
strategies. One of the strengths of this approach is adaptability;
it can effectively handle changes within the system, adapt-
ing to dynamic fluctuations in traffic patterns and resource
availability as they arise in the network. In [194], the authors
presented a DRL-driven architecture for a mixed-integer non-
linear programming (MINLP) problem to jointly optimize
resource allocation and computation offloading in an aerial-to-
ground (A2G) network. The proposed approach is model-free
DRL, which enabled the system to learn the optimal policy
in a dynamic environment by using past experience rather
than relying on knowledge of the underlying system model.

A multi-agent RL (MARL) algorithm was proposed in [195]
by the authors to optimize radio resources, computational
capacities, and AAV trajectories for hierarchical NTNs specifi-
cally designed for disaster relief services. The main aim of the
proposed framework is to maximize the number of satisfactory
connections with the constraint of tight end-to-end latency
constraints. The authors used an LSTM-based mechanism
LSTM that allowed the system to encode and exploit the
prior observation as well as the prior action in the transaction
history of the network for better accuracy and efficiency in
decision-making. The experimental results, particularly regard-
ing connection quality and system scalability, demonstrated
that the proposed algorithm significantly outperformed its
competitors, especially in scenarios with substantial increases
in AAVs and IIoT nodes. Such scalability in the solution
makes it appropriate for large-scale deployments in disaster
scenarios where speed and flexibility are critical for rapid
response. The work in [196] presented a satellite-assisted
ground-integrated network architecture that integrated LEO
satellites, AAVs, and cloud servers to provide edge computing
services for ground users when there is no infrastructure.
The authors formulated several optimization problems that
minimized both energy consumption and latency within the
network. They proposed a MADRL algorithm, to address the
very challenging problem of hybrid discrete-continuous action
spaces and focused on long-term optimization objectives.
In detailed simulation studies, the proposed algorithm has
demonstrated superior performance for each agent compared
to some benchmark methods. The achieved simulation results
were found to show superior improvements in terms of energy
consumption, latency, and the execution time of the task. The
proposed solution proved effective in a satellite-assisted edge-
computing environment, addressing the specific needs of such
systems.
In [197], the authors proposed a multi-task resource schedul-
ing (MRS) framework, based on a DRL foundation that
was devised for minimizing the total energy consumption of
an enhanced AAV-assisted MEC system with reconfigurable
intelligent surfaces (RIS). RISs are utilized to improve the
quality of communications between UEs and AAVs and to
more efficiently use resources. It used an A2C structure that
covered a multi-head agent, a multi-task controller, and a
light wolf search algorithm to optimize different parameters
such as the positioning of AAVs, phase-shifted diagonal
matrices, computation offloading, and resource allocation.
The results of the study showed that the multi-agent RS
(MARS) framework outperformed benchmarks significantly.
In [198], a GEO satellite-assisted vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V)
communication network was discussed as an optimization
problem for jointly optimizing task assignment, scheduling,
and resource management for communication and computing
tasks by minimizing the long-term weighted sum latency of
multitasking operations. To address this issue, the authors
proposed a DRL-based solution, which modeled the problem
of task scheduling and assignment as an MDP and then used a
DQL algorithm to solve it. The simulations conducted verified
both the convergence and effectiveness of the algorithm in
terms of latency reduction and overall improvement in system
performance. This solution has great potential to be deployed
in V2V communication networks where low-latency and high-
reliability communication are of paramount importance for the
safe and efficient running of vehicles.
The work in [199] introduced a new task offloading and
resource allocation strategy in the context of space-terrestrial
integrated optical transmission (STIOT) networks. The authors
combined DDPG and Lagrange multiplier algorithms to
attain optimal resource allocation and used the Karush-Kuhn-
Tucker (KKT) conditions. The network’s objective was defined
in terms of minimizing latency and energy consumption.
Leveraging powerful optimization techniques, the authors
proposed a novel approach that significantly reduced task
execution times and energy consumption, making it highly
suitable for space-terrestrial networks requiring real-time pro-
cessing and resource efficiency. In [200], the authors proposed
an end-to-end video analytics framework that joined MEC and
blockchain technology to optimize transaction throughput and
reduce the latency of applications based on Internet-of-AVs
(IoAVs), like surveillance video. The proposed solution used
an A3C-based algorithm that efficiently handled offloading
video and resource allocation within a decentralized network.
Indeed, with the A3C-based algorithm, an optimum solution
for the most suitable reward function was discovered because
it considered important factors such as the size of data,
CPU cycles, and latency, which allowed maximum potential
throughput for system efficiency with a minimal delay in real-
time video surveillance in AV networks.

design and operation of MEC systems deployed in NTNs. DRL
presents an exciting route for optimizing energy consumption
in the MEC-enabled non-terrestrial environment by learning
adaptive policies that minimize energy use while satisfying
the prescribed performance. In this subsection, we review
the literature on DRL-based solutions for EE enhancement
in MEC deployments under diverse non-terrestrial scenarios:
satellite networks, aerial drones, and AAVs. We will also
review how dynamically DRL algorithms operate on power
consumption management, optimize resource utilization, and
perform task scheduling to improve EE without degrading
any network performance. This section will review the state-
of-the-art techniques in leveraging DRL for energy-efficient
MeNT-WiNs through synthesizing insights across a range of
studies.

such as the positioning of AAVs, phase-shifted diagonal
matrices, computation offloading, and resource allocation.

communication network was discussed as an optimization
problem for jointly optimizing task assignment, scheduling,
and resource management for communication and computing
tasks by minimizing the long-term weighted sum latency of
multitasking operations. To address this issue, the authors
proposed a DRL-based solution, which modeled the problem
of task scheduling and assignment as an MDP and then used a
DQL algorithm to solve it. The simulations conducted verified
both the convergence and effectiveness of the algorithm in
terms of latency reduction and overall improvement in system
performance. This solution has great potential to be deployed
in V2V communication networks where low-latency and high-
reliability communication are of paramount importance for the
safe and efficient running of vehicles.

resource allocation strategy in the context of space-terrestrial
integrated optical transmission (STIOT) networks. The authors
combined DDPG and Lagrange multiplier algorithms to
attain optimal resource allocation and used the Karush-Kuhn-
Tucker (KKT) conditions. The network’s objective was defined
in terms of minimizing latency and energy consumption.
Leveraging powerful optimization techniques, the authors
proposed a novel approach that significantly reduced task
execution times and energy consumption, making it highly
suitable for space-terrestrial networks requiring real-time pro-
cessing and resource efficiency. In [200], the authors proposed
an end-to-end video analytics framework that joined MEC and
blockchain technology to optimize transaction throughput and
reduce the latency of applications based on Internet-of-AVs
(IoAVs), like surveillance video. The proposed solution used
an A3C-based algorithm that efficiently handled offloading
video and resource allocation within a decentralized network.
Indeed, with the A3C-based algorithm, an optimum solution
for the most suitable reward function was discovered because
it considered important factors such as the size of data,
CPU cycles, and latency, which allowed maximum potential
throughput for system efficiency with a minimal delay in real-
time video surveillance in AV networks.
B. EE
EE and sustainability continue to be the major issues in the
design and operation of MEC systems deployed in NTNs. DRL
presents an exciting route for optimizing energy consumption
in the MEC-enabled non-terrestrial environment by learning
adaptive policies that minimize energy use while satisfying
the prescribed performance. In this subsection, we review
the literature on DRL-based solutions for EE enhancement
in MEC deployments under diverse non-terrestrial scenarios:
satellite networks, aerial drones, and AAVs. We will also
review how dynamically DRL algorithms operate on power
consumption management, optimize resource utilization, and
perform task scheduling to improve EE without degrading
any network performance. This section will review the state-
of-the-art techniques in leveraging DRL for energy-efficient
MeNT-WiNs through synthesizing insights across a range of
studies.
In [161], the authors introduced a novel architecture for
integrated satellite-aerial-terrestrial relay networks (ISATRNs)
that utilized HAPs with AAVs equipped with RIS to enhance
EE and optimize system performance. The authors aimed
to maximize the system’s ergodic rate by jointly optimiz-
ing AAV trajectory, RIS phase shift, and active transmit
beamforming matrix while considering AAV energy con-
sumption constraints. To address this inherently complex
optimization problem, they proposed a DRL-based frame-
work using an improved LSTM-DDQL algorithm. The results
indicated that their proposed method outperformed traditional
DDQL algorithms in terms of single-step exploration average
reward values and other performance metrics, demonstrating
significant potential for practical applications in enhancing
the reliability and efficiency of next-generation ISATRNs.
The authors in [201] presented an optimization framework
for enhancing EE in multiple aerial RIS-assisted downlink
communication systems. By leveraging the advantages of
AAV deployment and RIS technology, the study addressed
poor line-of-sight issues between UE and BS. The authors
proposed a joint optimization problem encompassing RIS
deployment, reflecting elements’ on/off states, phase shift,
and power control, which is complex due to its mixed-
integer, non-convex, and NP-hard nature. This problem is
decomposed into three sub-problems, solved alternately using
successive convex approximation (SCA), actor-critic-PPO,
and the whale optimization algorithm. Extensive simulations
demonstrated the proposed algorithms’ efficacy, significantly
improving EE compared to several benchmark schemes. Ying
Chen et al. [202] proposed a distributed online task offloading
and resource allocation algorithm to minimize the energy
consumption of ground devices by reducing the drift-plus-
penalty function in each time slot in an aerial-MEC system
supported by HAPs and AAVs, using stochastic optimization
techniques and game theory. The distributed online task
offloading and resource allocation algorithm is shown to have
the lowest energy consumption and smallest queue backlog
compared to other algorithms, reducing energy consumption
by 15.73%–19.09% and queue backlog by 15.99%–88.84%.
In [203], the authors proposed a multi-AAV-assisted MEC
network incorporating a digital twin (DT) layer to minimize
the weighted energy consumption of mobile users and AAVs,
while ensuring that the task delay requirements are met. The
study employed a MARL approach based on multi-agent PPO
(MAPPO) with a Beta distribution and an attention mech-
anism to achieve optimal computation offloading policies.
The performance of the MAPPO algorithm was evaluated
against other RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness
in reducing energy consumption and improving both fair-
ness and network stability. The work in [204] introduced a
AAV-aided MEC architecture for vehicular networks, which
utilized line-of-sight massive multiple-input–multiple-output
(mMIMO) transmission to minimize the weighted total energy
consumption of vehicles and aerial roadside units (ARSUs).
The energy consumption for vehicles and ARSUs in each
time slot, including offloading, downloading, and computation
tasks, was formulated as a multi-variable optimization problem
aimed at minimizing total energy consumption, subject to
physical layer constraints, time slot scheduling, and task
allocation. The study found that massive MIMO can mitigate
distance-dependent path loss and reduce unnecessary ARSU
mobility.
Ei et al. [205] proposed a two-stage, multi-AAV-assisted
edge computing system, where AAVs provided both comput-
ing and relaying services to mobile devices. They formulated
a joint task offloading, communication, and computation
resource allocation problem to minimize the energy consumed
by AAVs and mobile devices. In the proposed system, mobile
devices offloaded tasks to AAVs, which then relayed part of the
tasks to terrestrial BSs for further processing, while minimiz-
ing energy consumption under resource constraints and task
deadlines. Simulations demonstrated that the approach reduced
network energy consumption and outperformed baseline meth-
ods. In [206], the authors presented a novel priority-based
DRL approach, aimed at optimizing the trajectory plan-
ning, communication scheduling, charging schedules, and task
offloading (PD-TCCT) of a AAV in a MEC network to
maximize the EE of AAV. Simulations demonstrated the
efficacy of the AAV-MEC network, showcasing improved EE
and a reduced energy consumption ratio compared to various
baseline approaches.

offloading. The primary goal of these strategies was to

trajectory design and the configuration of virtual machines

a non-convex mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem,
making it challenging to solve directly. However, the DDPG
algorithm demonstrated its effectiveness by outperforming a
DQL-based algorithm in reducing latency. This performance
improvement is attributed to DDPG’s ability to process con-
tinuous input data and generate continuous action outputs,
making it more suitable for real-time AAV trajectory control.

network, AVs serve as the key components, training DNNs
locally on their onboard systems. To enhance overall network
efficiency, AVs periodically share their learned parameters
with edge servers, thereby reducing system-wide latency and
simultaneously maintaining data privacy. This decentralized
approach ensured that raw data never leaves the local devices,
mitigating the risk of data breaches. The AVs functioned
as intelligent agents, continuously sensing the state of the
wireless channels, the quality of the datasets they generated,
and the current packet error rates. Based on this information,

wireless channel selection, and the adjustment of CPU-cycle
frequency. The performance of the F-DQL algorithm was
evaluated against three variants: F-DQL without offloading

analysis showed that the complete F-DQL algorithm achieved
significant reductions in system latency, clearly outperforming
all three variants.

enabled users to offload computation tasks, thereby improving

optimization method combines the Lagrange multiplier tech-
nique with a DQL, enabling the system to make optimal
task-offloading decisions. The objective was to minimize total
system latency while ensuring the smooth operation of IoT
applications. Simulation results indicated that the proposed
combined approach resulted in a notable enhancement in
IoT network performance, reducing the latency associated
with task execution and data processing. Another relevant
study, [212], focused on latency optimization for hybrid GEO-
LEO satellite-assisted IoT networks. The authors proposed
a task offloading and multidimensional resource allocation
(TOMRA) algorithm, which integrates DRL with convex
optimization techniques to minimize both task offloading and
processing latency. The system architecture included both
inter-satellite cooperation (between GEO and LEO satellites)
and satellite-ground cooperation, creating a complex but
highly efficient network capable of meeting the demands
of IoT applications. Simulation results demonstrated that
the proposed TOMRA algorithm consistently outperformed
benchmark schemes, making it a promising solution for
latency-sensitive IoT applications in hybrid satellite networks.
