E. Security and Privacy
Security and privacy are assumed to be the topmost concerns
in MeNT-WiNs, where transmitting sensitive data and commu-
nication operations are prone to various kinds of threats and
attacks. This section presents one of the promising frameworks
that integrate MEC with DRL in view of improving security
and privacy. In general, with the use of DRL algorithms, MEC
systems can adaptively respond to evolving security threats and
effectively mitigate privacy risks while guaranteeing efficiency
in network operation. This section reviews the literature on
DRL-based solutions for ensuring security and privacy in
MeNT-WiNs. Specifically, it examines existing studies on
how DRL techniques detect or prevent security breaches,
safeguard user privacy, and ensure data transmission integrity
and confidentiality in non-terrestrial environments.
The authors in [221] have equipped a multi-agent DRL-
based framework for all disjointed spectrum access, energy
control, and resource management allocation to vehicles in
vehicular edge computing (VEC) networks while aiming
to achieve an optimal system processing delay and at the
same time maintaining the security and reliability of V2V
communication links. A DDQL is proposed to optimize the
joint SORA scheme in a VEC network, where multiple vehicle
users concurrently learn how to minimize system processing
delay and proceed to secrecy probability maximization. On
the other hand, Consul et al. [222], devised an efficient
secure MEC system using AAVs and non-orthogonal multiple
access (NOMA) schemes and further adopted an FL algorithm
to bolster the security of the system through blockchain
technology. This study concentrated on the physical layer of
security, while blockchain technology is recommended to be
useful for ensuring the transparency and traceability of the
data supplied by the user as a consensus mechanism.
The authors in [223] explored a privacy-enhanced
blockchain computing offloading framework for satellite-
ground DT networks that integrated multi-agent reinforced
learning and Lyapunov stability theory to reduce execution
energy and privacy time overhead. A distributed RL algorithm
is employed to minimize the privacy protection costs and the
power consumption of the system whereby a Lyapunov drift
plus penalty is utilized on nested FL to update the weights
of actor networks to compute optimal offloading strategies.
Their proposed approach outperformed the benchmark strate-
gies by achieving the least execution energy overhead, the
highest quantity of bits processed, and the least privacy time
overhead. Lu et al. [224], investigated secure transmission
methods for multi-UAV-assisted MEC networks by employing
single-agent and MARL schemes. They aimed to determine
optimal AAVs’ locations and accomplish overall system load
offloading without compromising the overall system utility
by combining several users’ tasks which have some varying
requirements on computing hardware’s leftover energy and
delay. The QL-based single agent task offloading scheme
incorporates a Q table used to store each action taken, the
state of that action, and the expected reward of that action
being performed for each state-action pair. The agent picks
such action that corresponds to a maximum value of Q.
The multi-agent scheme based on Nash QL is employed to
optimize the secure offloading, where each agent updates its
Q-table according to the feedback of the environment through
continuous interaction with the environment. The multi-agent
method outperformed the single-agent and random offloading
schemes in terms of system and energy utility, however, it
accumulated a longer total delay.
F. Network Optimization
Network optimization is essential for maximizing the effi-
ciency, performance, and reliability of communication systems
in non-terrestrial environments, where dynamic conditions
and resource constraints pose significant challenges. MEC
combined with DRL is a promising paradigm toward network
operation optimization for overall improvements in system
performance. MEC systems can leverage DRL algorithms to
enable dynamic and adaptive reconfiguration of network set-
tings, resource allocation, and routing strategies, ensuring that
the network can adapt to changing demands and environmental
conditions over time. In this regard, we review the related
literature about network optimization strategies driven by DRL
in the case of MeNT-WiNs. We present how several DRL
techniques can be leveraged to optimize network efficiency,
scalability, and robustness in non-terrestrial environments,
surveyed from existing studies, paving the way for advanced
communication systems and services.
In [225], the authors proposed a MEC-empowered air-
ground integrated network (AGIN) framework where AAVs
act as edge servers to provide efficient computation services
for IoT devices and UE. A MADDPG-based strategy was
developed to jointly optimize task deployment and offload-
ing, addressing factors such as task placement, replacement,
offloading decisions, resource allocation, and power control.
The MADDPG framework achieved convergence and demon-
strated superior performance in simulations compared to the
baseline algorithms. In [226], the authors introduced a DRL-
based algorithm aimed at maximizing the sum computation
rate in a wireless-powered multi-access point edge computing
network consisting of multiple HAPs and IoT devices. These
IoT devices can harvest radio frequency energy from HAPs for
local data processing or offload tasks to the HAP edge servers.
The proposed algorithm optimized the offloading decision
and time allocation in this wireless-powered edge computing
system. Simulation results indicated that the algorithm per-
formed comparably to supervised learning techniques without
needing optimal samples and outperformed algorithms such as
DQL and AC in terms of computation rate and computational
complexity, especially in large-scale network settings.

In [228], the authors investigated the MEC paradigm for

while ensuring learning accuracy and energy consumption.

MEC system’s model decision, resource allocation, and tra-
jectory control simultaneously. The Iterative method alternates
between solving three subproblems, each of which is convex
or approximate convex. The proposed scheme achieved lower
service latency and better accuracy performance compared

can offer great service performance while adhering to energy
consumption, latency, and accuracy requirements.

rupt the communication link between the AAV and a BS

modeled as agents in an MDP to jointly optimize AAV
hover point selection, task collection time ratio, transmission
power, channel selection, and task offloading ratio to improve
communication and computing efficiency while considering
total AAV power and channel availability constraints. The

achieved optimal efficiency with improvements in reward and
task throughput by over 15% and 30%, respectively, compared

framework based on DRL to minimize energy consumption in

framework, which combined an actor-critic structure with a

search algorithm, optimized the positions of AAVs, phase-
shifted diagonal matrix, computation offloading, and resource
allocation. The superior performance of the proposed algo-
rithm is observed through various simulations when compared
with various existing benchmark schemes.

energy consumption of unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and

munication resources. The authors investigated a dual-layer
framework to solve the optimization problem by transforming
the original problem into a convex optimization problem and
then solving it using a dual-primal algorithm, and subsequently
solving the first-layer problem using a DRL algorithm. In order
to resolve the first formulation of the optimization problem,
a double-layered segmented decomposition framework was
used. The suggested Top-Algorithm provided a sub-optimal
solution of 88% in terms of optimality and hence reduced
the computational burden such that it outperformed other
existing DRL algorithms and baseline schemes in the total
energy consumption of the AAV-empowered M-IoT network.

agent FRL (MAFRL) algorithm to optimize power control,
user association, and resource allocation, in a AAV-empowered

the resource allocation and offloading decision in a AAV-
empowered MEC system, where each UE learns its own policy
to optimize the overall power consumption while satisfying
the latency constraint. The MAFRL algorithm achieved close
performance to a centralized MARL algorithm while pro-
tecting user privacy with Gaussian differentials and reducing
operation time by 23%. Table VI summarizes the literature

MeNT-WiNs. Collectively, these discussions demonstrate the

A. Computational Complexity and Scalability in
DRL-Empowered MeNT-WiNs
Applying DRL in MeNT-WiNs presents several formidable
challenges stemming from the inherent characteristics of non-
terrestrial environments. The spatiotemporal variability [232]
introduced by channel fading, mobility, and interference leads
to a highly dynamic and enlarged state space that agents
must learn and adapt to in near real-time. Furthermore,
URLLC requirements impose strict constraints on decision
latency and reliability, necessitating highly sample-efficient
learning and minimal exploration. The large-scale deploy-
ment of heterogeneous agents–such as AAVs, IoT nodes,
and satellites–with diverse roles and capabilities results in
massive scalability issues and a combinatorial explosion in
the joint action space [233]. Additionally, the limited onboard
computational and energy resources of these agents restrict
the frequency of model updates and necessitate lightweight
inference architectures. Moreover, partial observability [234]
and delayed or noisy feedback, due to decentralized coordi-
nation and asynchronous communications, further complicate
policy learning, making conventional DRL approaches less
effective in these settings. Below we discuss computa-
tional complexity and scalability challenges in DRL-assisted
MeNT-WiNs.

spans.content: 1) Computational Complexity: Applying DRL in non-
terrestrial networks, particularly in MeNT-WiNs, introduces
substantial computational complexity due to the high-
dimensional state and action spaces. This complexity is
further amplified by the dynamic topology, mobility of
AAVs and satellites, and time-varying wireless channel con-
ditions. Such characteristics impose significant computational
demands during both the training and inference phases of DRL
algorithms [235], [236]. The primary source of computational
load arises from the DNN operations–specifically, the forward
and backward propagations across multiple layers. To illustrate
this, consider the DDPG algorithm, where the actor network
is composed of an input layer, several hidden layers, and an
output layer.
Suppose that S denotes the dimensionality of the state space,
I is the number of neurons in the input of each layer, H is the
number of hidden layers, O is the number of neurons in the
output of each hidden layer, and A is the dimensionality of the
action space, respectively. The computational complexity for
processing the input layer is given by
S \times I ,
for the hidden
layers by
H \times I \times O ,
and for the output layer by
O \times A
. Thus,
the overall complexity of the actor network during inference
is expressed as [237], [238]
C _ {\mathrm{DDPG}} = S \times I + H \times I \times O + O \times A + A.
To analyze the scalability of DRL algorithms, we express
this using Big O notation. In computational complexity theory,
Big O notation
\mathcal { O } ( \cdot )
characterizes the upper bound of an
algorithm’s runtime or space usage with respect to input size.
It allows us to identify which operations dominate the overall
computational cost as the network scales. For DRL models,
this is especially useful in understanding how architectural
depth, layer width, and the dimensions of state and action
spaces impact performance. Given that
H \times I \times O
generally
dominates the other terms, i.e.,
H \times I \times O \gg S \times I , O \times A + A .
for deep networks, the above complexity expression simplifies
to
\begin{array}{l} C _ {\mathrm{DDPG}} = \mathcal {O} (S \times I + H \times I \times O + O \times A + A) \\ \approx \mathcal {O} (H \cdot I \cdot O). \\ \end{array}
This indicates that the computation is primarily driven by the
number of hidden layers and their interconnections.
This complexity analysis highlights how the neural
architecture and the size of the state-action space signifi-
cantly influence the inference cost. In MeNT-WiNs, where
real-time responsiveness and resource limitations are critical–
particularly for AAVs and LEO satellites–such computational
demands can be prohibitive. Therefore, strategies such as
model compression, knowledge distillation, and edge-assisted
DRL are essential to enable efficient and scalable deployment
under constrained environments.
2) Scalability: Regarding scalability, one of the primary
challenges is the state-space explosion problem in DRL mod-
els [239]. As the number of devices and operational states
in MeNT-WiNs grows, the dimensionality of the state and
action spaces increases exponentially. This leads to higher
computational requirements and prolonged convergence times
for DRL algorithms. The continuously changing network envi-
ronment necessitates frequent model updates, compounding
the computational complexity. Additionally, the computational
overhead of training and inference in DRL models, particularly
those employing DNNs, can overwhelm resource-constrained
platforms like satellites and AAVs. This often results in pro-
cessing delays and diminished responsiveness. Communication
latency between distributed MEC nodes, exacerbated by long
distances and high-latency links inherent to NTNs, further
hampers real-time decision-making.
Energy consumption presents another significant challenge.
The intensive computational demands of DRL algorithms can
rapidly deplete the limited power resources of AAVs and
satellites, necessitating efficient power management strategies
to ensure prolonged operation and sustained performance.
DRL training can be highly energy-intensive and computation-
ally demanding, especially when large deep neural networks
are involved [235]. While offline training in data centers
mitigates on-board computational costs, real-time adapta-
tion through online or continual learning–often necessary in
dynamic network environments–reintroduces significant over-
head. AAVs and satellites operating in MeNT-WiNs must
frequently update policies in response to changing channel
conditions, mobility events, and handovers, which may neces-
sitate partial on-board learning or frequent synchronization
with ground servers [240], [241]. Even during deployment,
deep model inference can be computationally expensive, par-
ticularly for policy optimization methods (e.g., PPO, SAC) and
value-based approaches (e.g., DQN), which rely on iterative
updates, gradient computations, and experience replay buffers.
In resource-constrained environments, even a forward pass
through a deep neural network can rapidly drain the limited
power resources of AAVs and satellites, particularly if infer-
ence is performed at high frequency [242], [243].
Furthermore, DRL systems frequently encounter issues
related to data sparsity and imbalance, as heterogeneous nodes
in MeNT-WiNs may provide non-uniform or limited data,
impairing model training and decision-making capabilities.
Moreover, the highly dynamic topologies of AAVs and satel-
lites result in continuously changing communication links
and coverage areas, requiring frequent policy adaptation in
real time [244]. Furthermore, intermittent connectivity due
to atmospheric conditions and orbital mechanics disrupts the
learning feedback loop, making consistent policy updates
challenging [241]. Unlike terrestrial networks, where DRL
agents can rely on stable infrastructure, MeNT-WiNs require
asynchronous learning and predictive modeling to mitigate
these disruptions. Another critical challenge is real-time adap-
tation, as rapid and unpredictable wireless channel variations
necessitate near-instantaneous decision-making. Additionally,
traditional DRL methods, which involve complex iterative
computations, may introduce unacceptable latency. Thus,
lightweight policy networks, edge-assisted DRL, or hybrid
model-based/model-free approaches are required to ensure
computational feasibility and responsiveness.

B. Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) in
MeNT-WiNs
ISAC is a new paradigm in wireless communication
networks where the same infrastructure serves for both com-
munication and environmental sensing. Clearly, such duality
is helpful in the context of MeNT-WiNs, where the spectrum,
power, and computation resources are scarce and must be
exploited efficiently. However, sensing-communication inte-
gration brings about significant challenges, especially in NTNs
where platforms like satellites and AAVs operate in dynamic
environments with resources that fluctuate. The central issue
to be addressed is how to make the various trade-offs between
sensing accuracy and communication performance in general,
especially when both functions need to be executed in parallel.
One of the most promising avenues for future research
involves the application of DRL algorithms to ISAC-enhanced
MeNT-WiNs, where DRL can be instrumental in optimiz-
ing the dual functionalities of sensing and communication,
enabling intelligent decision-making to balance competing
demands while ensuring fairness. As an example, a cer-
tain DRL algorithm may decide to give more emphasis to
communication tasks during low sensing demand, while in
other critical scenarios, such as natural disasters and search-
and-rescue missions, the resources should be shifted toward
sensing functions to grab essential data about the environment.

tum protocols tailored for MeNT-WiN environments, which

minimizing risks and accelerating innovation.

seamless two-way information exchange, and addressing the
computational overhead of creating and maintaining high-
fidelity virtual models. Additionally, the integration of DTs
with MeNT-WiNs require lightweight, scalable frameworks
capable of real-time operation. DRL can play a transformative
role in addressing these challenges and enhancing the func-
tionality of DTs within MeNT-WiNs. DRL can be employed to
develop intelligent decision-making frameworks for real-time
optimization of resource allocation and traffic management.

compression, reducing the computational burden of DTs while
preserving fidelity. DRL-driven solutions can also optimize the
interaction between physical network entities and their virtual
counterparts, enabling robust fault detection [262], predictive
maintenance [263], and enhanced energy management. Future
research should focus on creating DRL-assisted frameworks

efficient and resilient network operations.

J. EE in DRL-Enabled MeNT-WiNs
The integration of DRL into MeNT-WiNs presents signif-
icant challenges related to energy consumption, particularly
given the limited resources of platforms like AAVs, LEO
satellites, and HAPs. DRL algorithms, especially those involv-
ing deep NNs, require substantial computational resources for
both training and inference. The training phase, in particular,
is highly energy-intensive, as DRL models must process
large datasets and perform numerous iterations to update
their parameters. Similarly, the inference phase, where DRL
models make real-time decisions, can lead to high energy
consumption, especially on platforms with constrained power
budgets.
To address these energy challenges, several strategies can be
implemented. Model compression techniques, such as pruning
and quantization [245], can reduce the size and complexity
of DRL models, thereby decreasing computational require-
ments and energy usage during both training and inference.
Additionally, energy-aware resource allocation strategies can
be employed, where DRL itself can be used to optimize the
distribution of computational and communication tasks across
the network, minimizing energy consumption while still meet-
ing performance requirements. Another promising solution is
offloading tasks from energy-constrained nodes (like AAVs)
to more powerful edge servers or MEC nodes, which can
process the data without draining the local platform’s energy
reserves. Furthermore, the incorporation of FL into DRL
systems reduces the need for energy-intensive data transfers
by ensuring that only model updates (rather than raw data)
are shared between distributed nodes [264]. These techniques
enable DRL to be more energy-efficient, making it viable for
large-scale deployment in resource-constrained environments
like MeNT-WiNs.
K. Securing DRL-Enhanced MeNT-WiNs
While DRL offers substantial benefits in resource manage-
ment and system optimization, its integration into MeNT-WiNs
introduces several new security concerns that must be
addressed to ensure the robustness and reliability of these
networks. One of the primary risks is the vulnerability of
DRL models to adversarial attacks [265], where malicious
entities can manipulate the input data or training process to
cause the model to make suboptimal or harmful decisions. For
example, attackers could target the task offloading process in
a satellite network by manipulating network traffic to force a
DRL-based system into making inefficient resource allocation
decisions, leading to network congestion or service degrada-
tion. Similarly, data poisoning attacks could compromise the
learning process of DRL models by introducing erroneous data
into the system, corrupting the trained model, and reducing
the overall system reliability.
To mitigate these security threats, various solutions can
be employed. Secure FL [266] is one such approach, where
multiple agents collaboratively train DRL models without
sharing sensitive raw data, thus preserving privacy while
preventing malicious tampering. Additionally, anomaly detec-
tion systems powered by DRL [162] can continuously monitor
network traffic for unusual patterns or behaviors that may
indicate potential attacks, such as unauthorized access attempts
or DDoS attacks. DRL can also be used to enhance adaptive
security policies, dynamically adjusting encryption mecha-
nisms, access controls, and intrusion detection protocols [267]
in response to real-time network conditions or identified
threats. This adaptive approach allows MeNT-WiNs to respond
proactively to security challenges while maintaining high lev-
els of performance. By integrating robust security mechanisms
with DRL, MeNT-WiNs can ensure secure, efficient, and
resilient operations, safeguarding sensitive data and preventing
potential disruptions in non-terrestrial communication systems.

including HAPs, satellites, and AAVs. These platforms face
unique challenges such as intermittent connectivity, limited
energy and computation capabilities, long propagation delays,
and dynamic mobility. We discussed how DRL and MEC
facilitate adaptive resource allocation, mobility-aware task
offloading, and intelligent service orchestration under such
constraints. Furthermore, we illustrated how DRL can enhance
scalability, EE, and latency reduction in MeNT-WiNs through
case studies and recent works. This survey provided a detailed
roadmap for future research, offering insights into the evolving
landscape of DRL-assisted MeNT-WiNs and paving the way
for further innovation in intelligent, space-based wireless com-
munication systems. Addressing these challenges is essential
for achieving robust, real-world deployment of DRL in MeNT-
WiNs. Overall, this survey offered a structured roadmap for
future research and innovation in DRL-assisted MeNT-WiNs.
By bridging the gap between AI-driven decision-making and
next-generation wireless infrastructure, it aimed to inspire the
development of scalable, intelligent, and resilient communica-
tion systems across terrestrial and non-terrestrial domains.
